The through-line

One face.
One accent.
Everywhere.

A campaign is not a set of pieces that look similar — it is one system applied under different constraints. A poster has three seconds and a wall. A business card has a hand. A banner has 300 pixels. The same typeface, accent and spacing logic have to survive all three.

A commercial and a twenty-minute documentary are the same problem at different speeds: decide what the viewer should feel at each moment, then build the rhythm that gets them there. Cut for arc, grade for consistency, score to the edit — never the other way round.

6.1 — Manthan · visual development

8 locked frames

The stills the short film was built from

How these are made

Direction first.
The model comes fourth.

Nothing here was prompted once and accepted. Every image starts as a written brief — subject, lens, light source, time of day, mood — before a single generation runs. Look development happens before volume: lighting logic, palette, lens behaviour and grain are fixed on one frame, then held across every frame that follows.

From there it's reference chaining rather than re-rolling. A locked frame becomes the reference for the next, so a subject stays itself across a whole set instead of drifting. Frames that hold get a finishing pass in Photoshop and are upscaled before they go anywhere near a client deck.
